entries.section: (1) The preaching of Christ

paragraphs.text: St. Paul the Apostle always boasts and identifies himself as a servant, by his own will, of the Lord Christ, because He loved him first, called him, and chose him as an apostle by appearing to him Himself, and his mission is to preach the good news of the Gospel.

The apostleship of St. Paul opens a door of hope for us. As Christ chose him, He wishes to choose you also, beloved brother, in spite of your weak abilities and whatever your past life has been, to be His ambassador among your brethren by your conduct and your upright speech.

entries.section: (1) The preaching of Christ

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ is the center of the preaching, and He is the promise for which mankind longed greatly. How often the prophets spoke of Him as a man (the son of David), like us, sharing with us our suffering nature.

entries.section: (1) The preaching of Christ

paragraphs.text: The Spirit of holiness: The Holy Spirit, by the resurrection of Christ from the dead, revealed to us with power and clarity that He is also the living God who rose from the dead by Himself, by the power of His divinity. We believed in Him by the Holy Spirit who dwells in us, whom we received as the greatest gift through the sacrament of the Holy Myron after Baptism. For no one can say that Christ is Lord but by the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, my beloved brother, the soul rejoices in Him, for it finds in Him all its needs. He is Jesus the man, who feels with you and suffered as you do; He is Christ the Redeemer, who bore in your place the penalty of suffering and death; and He is the Lord God who rose from the dead, saying to you, beloved: "I have conquered the strongest enemy of mankind, which is death, so why are you afraid? Trust Me, for I am able to solve all your problems."

entries.section: (1) The preaching of Christ

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ offered the grace of redemption to all mankind, not because of any merit in us, but because of His love for us, since His delight is with the sons of Adam. He set the apostles apart to proclaim to all the Gentiles that they should accept the truths of the faith with obedience and complete submission from the heart.

entries.section: (1) The preaching of Christ

paragraphs.text: The Apostle Paul began by directing and addressing his words to the believers in Rome, calling them beloved of God, and saying that Christ calls them to a life of holiness, granting them peace and joy.

God calls you to a life of holiness if you obey His commandments, and your life is then filled with peace, that great grace of which the world today is deprived because of its evil. Indeed, the children of the world complain every day of depression and sleeplessness, for "There is no peace, saith the Lord, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22).

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the believers

paragraphs.text: It is remarkable in this verse that St. Paul rejoices in the faith of the Christians of Rome and thanks God for it, despite the lack of precision and depth in this faith, as we shall see later. But St. Paul teaches us to look for the virtues of others, and to thank God and praise them for these.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the believers

paragraphs.text: Here St. Paul draws our attention to the only worship acceptable before God, which is worship in the Spirit (Jn 4:23, 24). In it the believer walks according to the commandments of the Gospel, doing everything through Christ and for His sake, keeping in his heart that God sees all his deeds and the thoughts of his heart, even those that people do not see. Therefore the spiritual person always tries, as far as his strength allows, to please God's heart with love. This is the opposite of formal worship, in which a person is concerned with religiosity before people only, to obtain their praise, while his heart is empty of any love or fear of God.

And because St. Paul knew that the delight of God's heart is for sinners to return to the Father's embrace, his heart was kindled with a fatherly love, in imitation of his Christ as a shepherd who seeks His sheep. So Paul remembers the Christians of Rome at all times and prays for them, hoping to visit Rome to preach there and to strengthen the believers in it.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the believers

paragraphs.text: St. Paul declares his longing to come to them and see them, not to take anything for himself, but to give them a spiritual gift to strengthen them, in the form of preaching or guidance suited to each one.

entries.section: (2) Encouraging the believers

paragraphs.text: Here Paul concludes this section by saying that he will rejoice in their faith and they will rejoice in his faith. That is, the servant is encouraged by seeing faith in his children, just as those he serves are strengthened when they see the strength of their servant's faith.

Be careful to pray for those around you and those you know, near and far, confident that your prayer opens their hearts to the knowledge of God and strengthens them in it, in addition to deepening your own personal relationship with God first.

entries.section: (3) Paul's longing to preach in Rome

paragraphs.text: Here St. Paul affirms once more the extent of his longing for them, declaring that all the abilities and gifts he has he is ready to offer in his ministry and preaching among them, so that he may rejoice in the fruits of their faith and virtues, explaining that he is a debtor to God, who loved him and died for him. So he offers his love to God's children, mankind, whether Greeks or others (barbarians), and to the learned and the unlearned.
And you, beloved, if someone asks you for some service, do not look upon it as toil or effort, but rejoice, for every labor of love offered to God lays up for you a treasure in heaven.

entries.section: (3) Paul's longing to preach in Rome

paragraphs.text: Paul boasts that he preaches the Gospel of Christ and is not ashamed of His sufferings and crucifixion, because the Gospel has a power that works in souls. He began preaching to the Jews first, because they are Jews like him and know God and the prophets.

entries.section: (3) Paul's longing to preach in Rome

paragraphs.text: The righteousness of God: His justice and His mercy.

From faith to faith: Its origin is "from faith to faith." That is, the redemption of Christ transferred us from the first faith in the Old Testament, in which a person, in order to become righteous, had to do the works and commandments of the Law and offer many sacrifices, which were a symbol of Christ, to atone for his sins; to the second faith in the New Testament, which is built on trust in the infinite sacrifice of Christ the Redeemer on the Cross, which atones for the sins of mankind and so justifies those who believe in it.

The Gospel revealed to us the righteousness of God, which made us righteous before Him. When Christ died for us, He satisfied divine justice so that we might receive God's mercy and forgiveness. Not every person enjoys this justification, but only the one who lives by faith (Hab 2:4), that is, the one who believes and also obeys His commandments.

entries.section: (4) Rejecting God and idolatry

paragraphs.text: After Paul encouraged the believers in Rome and praised their faith, he declares God's wrath on the Gentiles who despise God and persist in their sins, and he rejects the sins by which the wicked suppress the truth and conceal it.

entries.section: (4) Rejecting God and idolatry

paragraphs.text: There is no excuse for a person who claims not to know God, because His voice is within him, and it is the conscience.

entries.section: (4) Rejecting God and idolatry

paragraphs.text: His invisible things: His divine power hidden behind His works.
The things that are made: the creatures.
Eternal: everlasting, without beginning or end.

For God's living creation, of man, animal, and plant, as well as the inanimate, such as the mountains, seas, planets, and stars, and the wonderful geometric order of nature, declares clearly that there must be a mighty and great God behind this amazing creation. So why do the pagans not believe? They have no excuse for their unbelief.

entries.section: (4) Rejecting God and idolatry

paragraphs.text: In their ignorance and stupidity, after they knew God, instead of thanking Him for His gifts, people attributed the credit for creation, the universe, and His gifts to idols made in the form of human beings, animals, or birds, and worshiped them.

Examine your heart: is it attached to God or to other idols such as money, position, or various desires? Do not remove God from your heart to put anyone or anything in His place, and review yourself at the end of every day: to what extent have you lived with God, and how much have you been occupied with worldly matters?

entries.section: (5) Giving license to uncleanness and fornication

paragraphs.text: When man replaced God with idols, which are false, unreal gods, God gave him up to uncleanness. That is, God left the wicked to do evil by their own will, in fornication and perversion by which they dishonored their pure bodies, and they forgot that they were created in the image and likeness of God, after their continual rejection of the work of God's grace. God allowed them to humble themselves, so that perhaps they might repent of their evil and return again to their purity.

entries.section: (5) Giving license to uncleanness and fornication

paragraphs.text: Because the wicked abandoned God, their vile passions humbled them, such as women turning away from the natural, holy sexual relations that God created, to perverse relations, whether a woman with a woman like herself, or sinful sexual practices with men, but not in the natural organs meant for procreation. Because of the hideousness of this sin, it is counted among the causes of divorce which the Church permits.

entries.section: (5) Giving license to uncleanness and fornication

paragraphs.text: The men were not content with the sin of fornication, but went beyond it to sexual perversion with one another, that abominable sin which greatly angered God against the people of Sodom, so that He burned it with fire long ago.

entries.section: (5) Giving license to uncleanness and fornication

paragraphs.text: God forbid that it be God who gave them up to evil with His own hands; rather, they fell by their own will, like a sick man who refused to listen to his doctor's advice, and so his condition worsened. And as a result of their sins they receive punishment, such as fornicators being afflicted with diseases like syphilis, AIDS, and cervical cancer.
But why does the merciful God allow this?
So that man may realize the effects and torment of sin and its deceit, that perhaps he may repent of it.

entries.section: (5) Giving license to uncleanness and fornication

paragraphs.text: Because of man's foolishness and stubbornness, instead of repenting of sin, he takes even more pleasure in it, forgetting its pains and its punishment. For this reason St. Paul mentioned this enormous number of sins, to show that a person usually begins with one sin, and that sin drags the rest of the sins after it, so that he is filled with all unrighteousness. The word unrighteousness means all sins in general.

entries.section: (5) Giving license to uncleanness and fornication

paragraphs.text: Whisperers: those who speak evil of people in secret.
Backbiters: those who speak evil and lies openly.
Slanderers: those who fall into judging others.
Boasters: that is, those who exaggerate in their words and attribute to themselves what they do not have.
Inventors of evil things: those who devise new kinds of evil.
Disobedient to parents: they refuse to learn, to be disciples, and to benefit from previous experience.

entries.section: (5) Giving license to uncleanness and fornication

paragraphs.text: Covenantbreakers: that is, one who does not keep his promises to others and does not carry them out. In sum, they are hard-hearted and ignorant.

entries.section: (5) Giving license to uncleanness and fornication

paragraphs.text: After the wicked knew God's wrath and His punishment of destruction for them, they did not repent but defied Him by encouraging others to sin, as happens now when the media present stimulating films, and young people encourage one another to smoke cigarettes and use drugs, and incite one another to sinful romantic relationships, and encourage sexual freedom as proof of their manhood or womanhood.

Therefore, beloved, beware of sin at all its levels, and beware of following the ideas of the world and its freedom, for the whole world lieth in wickedness. And if sin gains mastery over you, pray with faith to your God, who is able to free you from sins, and continue your spiritual striving against it.

Thus St. Paul concluded the chapter with a problem in need of a solution, the problem of the sinner sitting in the shadow of death who deserved God's wrath, and who is now in the utmost need of justification in Christ, through faith and by abandoning the works of darkness.
God the Judge

entries.section: (1) Judging others

paragraphs.text: St. Paul begins by directing his words to every person who thinks that his knowledge and understanding of God's law place him in a higher rank than other people, so that he judges them and pronounces others guilty as though he were a judge over their faults, while he finds dozens of excuses for himself when he falls into the same faults. He also warns us that the one who judges does those same things, that is, whoever judges another will certainly fall into the same sin one day because he has not been humble. Therefore the verse came plainly: "thou art inexcusable," and you will be subject to judgment, you who judge another.

entries.section: (1) Judging others

paragraphs.text: Here St. Paul reminds us of a fact we all know, which is that God's judgment is according to truth. That is, He judges not only by outward appearance but also examines the heart, knowing each person's motives for sin, taking into account the circumstances and environment in which the sinner grew up, aware of each person's measure of spiritual knowledge and whether he committed the sin willingly and intentionally or as a result of weakness. Thus the measure of God's punishment for the same sin differs from one person to another.

entries.section: (1) Judging others

paragraphs.text: Here St. Paul mentions a wrong behavior that psychologists know as "projection," in which the sinful person numbs his guilty conscience by talking a great deal about the faults of others.

Therefore, beloved, do not think that you are without sin so that you judge others. Do you know that not paying the tithes is the sin of theft, or that whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart, and that abortion is murder? Indeed, gossip itself is counted as a moral murder of the one you judge, because you distort his image before people. Therefore, beloved, instead of spending hours gossiping about others, hold yourself accountable instead for a few minutes daily for what you did throughout the day, and in this way you escape the judgment of God. And if you see your brother fallen, say to yourself: perhaps he will repent of it, while I may fall into it tomorrow.

entries.section: (2) The judgment of God

paragraphs.text: Because of the abundance of God's kindness and longsuffering toward your sins, do you despise His mercies, that is, does fear of Him disappear from your heart?!

entries.section: (2) The judgment of God

paragraphs.text: Does your heart grow harder, and do you persist in sin day after day, thus adding to the account of your sins new sins every day?

Therefore take heed, beloved, for God will reveal His wrath against those who did not make use of the period of His mercy and the time of His forgiveness throughout their life on earth. When their life ends, they will then receive a just punishment from God (Rev 20:11-15).

Perhaps you now also understand, beloved, why God is patient with the wicked who trouble you, and does not punish them now so that their harm to you might cease. The reason is that God's longsuffering includes all mankind, including you also, so that He may give everyone an equal opportunity to repent.

entries.section: (2) The judgment of God

paragraphs.text: This verse is plain and strongly declares that purely intellectual, theoretical faith alone is not enough to obtain salvation, but there must be good works, which will be the measure of recompense, since God asks of us a faith translated into good works (the doctrine of faith and works). This is a reply to some heresies that proclaim the sufficiency of faith alone for salvation. (Mt 16:27, 2 Cor 5:10, Jas 2:17-24, Rev 2:23.)

entries.section: (2) The judgment of God

paragraphs.text: Here St. Paul affirms the importance of works once more, explaining the reward of those who persevere in good work with all patience, without slackness or weariness, desiring not the glory, honor, and positions of the passing, false world, but true glory in eternal life, when God wipes every tear from their eyes, crowns them with a crown of glory and honor, and satisfies them with what eye has not seen and ear has not heard.

entries.section: (2) The judgment of God

paragraphs.text: St. Paul brings us back once more to the contentious, who are from the fanatical Jewish party, who do not follow the truth but incline in their hearts and conduct toward sin; these will reap the indignation and wrath of God upon themselves. He explains that the cause of evil is distance from God (they do not obey the truth), just as the source of goodness is faith and obedience to God.

entries.section: (2) The judgment of God

paragraphs.text: Here he puts the wicked among the Jews before the wicked among the Gentiles in receiving punishment, because the Jews received more privileges than the Gentiles in spiritual knowledge.

entries.section: (2) The judgment of God

paragraphs.text: St. Paul puts the righteous among the Jews before the righteous repentant among the Gentiles in glory and honor, because they knew God before them, and so they labored and grew spiritually more than the Gentiles who returned to God.

entries.section: (2) The judgment of God

paragraphs.text: God shows no partiality to anyone. Whoever received more spiritual knowledge from God is punished more if he is wicked, and rewarded more if he is righteous, for his striving after knowledge and carrying out the truth.

Imitate God in not showing partiality. If someone appeals to you in some problem, judge according to the truth, and do not favor your relatives or friends. How many marriages have been destroyed because each party and his family did not judge justly and did not admit their faults, casting all the blame and condemnation on the other party.

entries.section: (3) Conscience and the Law

paragraphs.text: After St. Paul spoke of the justice of God, he answered for us a question that puzzled people for a long time: how will God judge the Gentiles although they did not receive the Law, that is, the law of Moses, as the Jews did? And what is the fault of children born to Gentile fathers and raised far from the knowledge of the law of Moses? The answer is that God has provided the Gentiles with a natural law, which is the conscience. Every person is born by nature equipped with this moral law, and the written law of Moses is in reality nothing but a bringing out of the law of conscience written on the tablets of the heart. Therefore, while the erring Jew is judged according to the law of Moses, the Gentiles who are without the law, that is, without the law of Moses, are judged according to the law of conscience. And the phrase "shall also perish without law" means that the Mosaic law will not be a witness against him.

entries.section: (3) Conscience and the Law

paragraphs.text: It is obvious that those who know and understand the commandments of the Law are not the righteous, as the Jews thought, but those who carry out the commandments of the Law, whether the law of Moses or the law of conscience.

entries.section: (3) Conscience and the Law

paragraphs.text: The Gentiles who do not have the law of Moses, when they do by nature the commandments that are in the law of Moses, that is, spontaneously from within their own consciences, and become obedient to God, their conscience becomes their law, because conscience is a voice from God in man.

entries.section: (3) Conscience and the Law

paragraphs.text: In this St. Paul has praised some of the Gentiles who, by their good works, showed and proved that God's natural law is written on their hearts more deeply than it was written on the two tablets of stone for the Jews.

Their conscience also bearing witness: Just as the law of Moses will be the witness against the Jew on the Day of Judgment, so the conscience of the Gentile will be a witness to the thoughts of his heart, which are divided into two parties:
A party that accuses (accuse), that is, reproves the person for wrong deeds.
A party that excuses (excuse), that is, finds an excuse for the person for his wrong deeds.

Perhaps this is the eternal struggle in man between good and evil. And the conscience here is the witness over man as to who prevailed: the accusing thoughts of good, or the excusing thoughts of evil?

entries.section: (3) Conscience and the Law

paragraphs.text: This judgment will take place on the Day of Judgment when God judges the secrets, that is, the secrets of hearts and hidden sins, but by a greater standard, which is according to the commandments of the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

If you have enjoyed the knowledge of Christ and His commandments, be careful to live in Him lest you be judged on the last day, especially when you find that some non-Christians have applied these commandments under the guidance of their conscience.

entries.section: (4) The judgment of the Jews

paragraphs.text: St. Paul mocks the duplicity of Christians of Jewish origin, for they teach one thing and do another. They did not rely on the blood of Christ the Redeemer but on being Jews of the chosen people, whom God set apart as a people dedicated to Himself, and distinguished among all the peoples of the earth by giving them the Law written by the finger of God on the tablets of the Law.

entries.section: (4) The judgment of the Jews

paragraphs.text: He also rebukes their reliance on their knowledge of God, and their discerning of the things that differ, that is, the difficult issues of religion, such as love of God and fear of Him, mercy and leniency, firmness and severity... and so on.

entries.section: (4) The judgment of the Jews

paragraphs.text: By abundance of knowledge you became a guide of the blind, that is, the ignorant in spiritual knowledge, and a light to those in darkness, that is, the Gentiles living in the darkness of sin.

entries.section: (4) The judgment of the Jews

paragraphs.text: The Apostle Paul continues his rebuke of the Jews for their outward show, since the Jew considers himself:

An instructor of the foolish: that is, a teacher of those who are ignorant of the knowledge of God, guiding them to the truth. A teacher of babes: since classes were held in the synagogue to teach the young.
The form of knowledge and of the truth: The Jew is concerned that his outward appearance should show that he is great in knowledge and truth.

entries.section: (4) The judgment of the Jews

paragraphs.text: What hypocrisy and deceit by which you deceive yourself and others! You command people to abstain from sins like theft and adultery, and you abhor, that is, you call for hatred of, idols, yet you permit yourself theft and adultery and the robbing of the costly idols found in the temple of the pagans.

entries.section: (4) The judgment of the Jews

paragraphs.text: You boast that you know and respect the Law, but by transgressing the commandments of the Law and not carrying them out, you dishonor God Himself, because you give no weight to His word.

entries.section: (4) The judgment of the Jews

paragraphs.text: The final result of this is that unbelievers blaspheme, that is, they deny the religion that God established, and even reject God Himself because of your conduct.

Examine yourself, my brother, lest you be a stumbling block to others, and what you teach others, make sure that you try to apply it first in your own life, so that your teaching will be deeper and more powerful and more convincing to those who hear you.

entries.section: (5) Circumcision does not justify

paragraphs.text: Circumcision profits the Jew if he does the commandments of the Law, but if he is a transgressor, that is, one who does not carry out the commandments, he has become like a Gentile who does not know God, that is, uncircumcised (not circumcised).

entries.section: (5) Circumcision does not justify

paragraphs.text: If the uncircumcised Gentile keeps the Law, he is truly counted as one of the circumcised children of God.

entries.section: (5) Circumcision does not justify

paragraphs.text: The uncircumcised, who keeps the commandments of the Law out of his conscience, will be a judge of the circumcised Jew, who knows God's commandments and does not carry them out.

entries.section: (5) Circumcision does not justify

paragraphs.text: Then who is the true Jew? Of course, he is the one whom God praises.
For the word Jew in Hebrew means (praise), and for what does God praise him? Of course not for the circumcision of the flesh.

entries.section: (5) Circumcision does not justify

paragraphs.text: The one whom God praises is the one whose heart is circumcised, that is, from whom sin and iniquity have been removed by the knife of the Holy Spirit, and not only whose body is circumcised according to the commandment of Scripture. This is the true Jew, who seeks the praise of God and not the praise of people.

In short, beloved, do not rely on some outward appearances in formal worship so that people may praise you, but let your outward worship be joined to worship of the heart and purity of heart. And do not boast that you are an Egyptian from among the sons of the martyrs, and that your country was visited by the Holy Family, and that it has many monasteries and shrines, but see whether your works glorify God and gladden His heart and the hearts of those martyrs?!
Justification by faith and not by the works of the Law

entries.section: (1) What is the benefit of circumcision?

paragraphs.text: St. Paul begins this chapter with a question: if neither the Law nor circumcision justifies a person, why did God ask for it from the days of Abraham and Moses?

entries.section: (1) What is the benefit of circumcision?

paragraphs.text: The Law and circumcision have many benefits, since God entrusted the Jews with His words and commandments, that they might keep them intact for all mankind. And in truth they were equal to the responsibility, but with formality and literalism in applying it.

entries.section: (1) What is the benefit of circumcision?

paragraphs.text: St. Paul declares that man's unfaithfulness does not nullify the power and soundness of the commandment; the defect is not in the commandment but in man's inability to carry it out.

entries.section: (1) What is the benefit of circumcision?

paragraphs.text: The word of God is always true, while man's objection and doubt is the lie, as was said in the Psalm (51:4). In His humility, God allows us to examine His words so as to discover their power and soundness. If man examines God's word in order to judge it, he will discover that God's word is righteous and true and overcomes all the arguments and words of men.

Do not hasten to murmur against God, because you are a limited creature and His wisdom is higher than your mind, and all His commandments are necessary for your life. Ask for His help and guidance, and you will understand and be able to apply His commandments; indeed, in proportion to your submission to His word, He reveals to you His wisdom in the ordering of your affairs.

entries.section: (2) Does doing evil glorify God??

paragraphs.text: Here St. Paul expresses astonishment and condemns the saying of people who toy with the idea that God's righteousness is displayed with sinners and fornicators: the harder the illness, the more the skill of the physician appears, and the more the iniquity increases, the more the competence of God appears in healing, sanctifying, and justifying. Then people say, "God who taketh vengeance" on us as a punishment for our sins "is unrighteous," because by our sins we displayed His righteousness, so He ought to reward us instead of punishing.

entries.section: (2) Does doing evil glorify God??

paragraphs.text: Here St. Paul condemned that idea by saying: how could God, the just Judge, be unrighteous?

entries.section: (2) Does doing evil glorify God??

paragraphs.text: St. Paul repeated the people's words in his own voice: "The more we lie and sin, the more the angels and the righteous glorify God for the greatness of His mercy and power." Then why am I still judged as a sinner when I am the cause of the glorifying of God?

entries.section: (2) Does doing evil glorify God??

paragraphs.text: Slanderously reported: that which we did not say is said in our name, and erroneous speech is attributed to us.

The Apostle Paul declares his distress at those who attributed to him a saying he did not say, namely: "Let us do evil" so that God will have mercy on us and give us good things, and so His holy name is glorified. It is as though Paul permitted the doing of iniquity. These in truth deserve judgment for this fallacy.

Beware, beloved, of this dangerous idea, for it calls for moral and spiritual laxity. God's mercy does not relieve the sinner of his full responsibility, by his will, for committing sin. So it is better for you to try from now to walk in the way of truth, to train yourself in doing good, so that people may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

entries.section: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

paragraphs.text: So that Christians of Jewish origin may not boast and say, "We are better than Christians of Gentile origin," St. Paul replies, denying that, and reminds them that he has declared in (chapters 1 and 2) that Jews and Gentiles have all sinned.

entries.section: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

paragraphs.text: "As it is written": All the coming verses from verse (10) to verse (19) are verses from the Old Testament describing the sins of the Jewish people, which St. Paul quotes here to prove by them that they were a people who greatly provoked God.

St. Paul began with the verse "there is none that doeth good, no, not one" (Ps 14:3). Even the saints in the Old Testament had their faults, and those of whom Scripture said that they were righteous, like Elizabeth and Zacharias, had an imperfect righteousness, because Christ had not yet accomplished redemption. Therefore, when the righteous died, they went to Hades even though they were righteous, and did not enter Paradise until after the crucifixion and death of Christ. Only then did they begin to enjoy complete justification.

entries.section: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

paragraphs.text: This verse, from Ps (53:2), shows that the Jews preserved the verses and words of the Law, but did not understand the purpose behind them, and did not love God from their hearts, which is the goal of the Law.

entries.section: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

paragraphs.text: Gone out of the way: they went far away and turned aside from the way of truth.
God shows in (Ps 14:3) that all have fallen into corruption, and not even one good person was found.
There are sins that are widespread and prevailing in the society around you; do not be swept into them because many have fallen into committing them.

entries.section: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

paragraphs.text: Asps: serpents.

God declares in (Ps 5:9) that the mouth of the wicked, which speaks plots and false testimonies, was the cause of the killing of many innocent people, and they are like serpents, speaking with cunning and hypocrisy, as if they were friends, but their tongue carries deadly danger.
Here ask yourself: is your tongue a cause of blessing for others, or a cause of harm and bitterness for them?

entries.section: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

paragraphs.text: Here Paul cites the words of the Psalm (Ps 10:7), which shows how sinners curse everyone and murmur against everything.
Beware of murmuring, and do not think that God has singled you out for the greatest share of the world's calamities, but thank Him for the many good things He bestows upon you.

entries.section: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

paragraphs.text: Isaiah shows in (Isa 59:7, 8) the swiftness of the wicked in killing others. They were not content with robbery, that is, stealing from others, but worked to crush and shatter them, like King Ahab, who killed Naboth the Jezreelite in order to seize his field. As a result of all these deeds, they lost their inner peace, "There is no peace, saith the Lord, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22).

entries.section: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

paragraphs.text: The Psalm (36:1) reveals the reason for these sins, which is that they did not set the fear of God before them when they were committing them.

entries.section: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

paragraphs.text: Destruction: divine punishment.

It is obvious that what the Law said in the preceding verses is directed to those who are under the Law, that is, the Jews, so that every Jewish mouth may be stopped and they have no argument with which to defend themselves by their mouths. Thus the whole world in both its parts, Jews and Gentiles, becomes deserving of punishment and death from God.

entries.section: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

paragraphs.text: Before Him: that is, before the Law, because the Law made us know the meaning of sin, as though it were a book of statutes and penalties that came to regulate the life of man, who had lived without a religion to restrain him or a law to deter him. So every person found himself unrighteous because he fell short in carrying out the commandments of the Law.

entries.section: (4) Justification by God's grace

paragraphs.text: But now the righteousness of God, which was accomplished by redemption, has been manifested to us and we have seen it. It is the turning point in the spiritual history of mankind without the Law, so that salvation became possible without the need for the works of the Law such as circumcision and blood sacrifices. And this righteousness through the redemption of Christ is not a new idea to mankind; rather, all the prophets spoke of it, and all the ordinances of the Law, the rites, and the sacrifices pointed to it and prepared the way for it.

entries.section: (4) Justification by God's grace

paragraphs.text: The righteousness of God by faith: that is, the salvation offered to mankind so that we may believe in it. Unto all: that is, every soul, whether Jew or Gentile; there is no difference with God.

entries.section: (4) Justification by God's grace

paragraphs.text: All people were equal before God in regard to their sins, which caused man to lose his glory as one like God, in His image and likeness, so that man became in the utmost need and want of his lost glory.

entries.section: (4) Justification by God's grace

paragraphs.text: Christ bore all our sins and died for us, and in this we are justified freely if we believe in His redemption.

entries.section: (4) Justification by God's grace

paragraphs.text: This justification by the blood of Christ also works retroactively, to atone for our past sins, or the sins of those who died in the faith awaiting Christ the Savior.

entries.section: (4) Justification by God's grace

paragraphs.text: God's plan from eternity is the justification and redemption of man, and this was accomplished by the crucifixion of Christ. God is righteous from eternity to eternity, but by His death He justified everyone who believes in Him.

entries.section: (4) Justification by God's grace

paragraphs.text: The Jew must not boast of having accomplished the works of the Law, because they did not justify him; rather, he was justified by his faith in Christ.

entries.section: (4) Justification by God's grace

paragraphs.text: God is certainly the God of the Jews and of the Gentiles.

entries.section: (4) Justification by God's grace

paragraphs.text: The just God is one for all, justifying all by faith in Him, whether the circumcised Jew or the uncircumcised Gentile.

entries.section: (4) Justification by God's grace

paragraphs.text: All this does not nullify or abolish the place and importance of the Law in the Old Testament, for it was a preparation for the salvation that Christ accomplished on the Cross, and our faith in Christ the Redeemer establishes the Law, which was necessary to prepare man so that he might know sin and reject it, and then Christ comes and removes it from him.

Believe in God's power that forgives your sins however many they are, and ask His help to free you from the hardest sins, and be confident that God rejoices in your repentance, your seeking of Him, and your striving to drive out sins and keep away from them. But on the other hand, do not depend on your intelligence and abilities alone to give up sins, but believe in God and ask for His support, and do all that is in your power, and you will receive forgiveness and peace.
Abraham is justified by faith

entries.section: (1) Abraham was justified by his faith

paragraphs.text: Hath found: obtained righteousness and salvation.
St. Paul asks what Abraham gained from his works according to the flesh, and whether he obtained righteousness by them? No, as he will answer in the following verses.

entries.section: (1) Abraham was justified by his faith

paragraphs.text: If Abraham's good works were what justified him, he would have the right to boast of them before people. But in truth he was not justified in God's sight by works, and when God justified him He did not mention that He justified him because of his works; rather, Scripture says that when Abraham believed God, only then did God count him righteous. And this is certainly grace, that God should count a person as righteous.

Abraham did not need the works of the Law, because it had not yet appeared. So he declares that the works of the Law are not needed for a person to be justified. This is, of course, different from the good works resulting from faith, in which we live now.

Our talk about Abraham's faith must not make us forget the importance of his works. St. James said in his epistle: "Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar? Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?" (Jas 2:21-23).

entries.section: (1) Abraham was justified by his faith

paragraphs.text: Him that worketh: the works of the Law.
Grace: a free gift that gives salvation, justification, and entrance into the Kingdom.
Debt: God is in debt to give something in return for man's toil as his wages, which are material blessings on earth, but they do not forgive his sins nor does he enter the Kingdom.

St. Paul completes the answer to the question in verse (v. 1), saying that whoever deals with God only on the basis of his works according to the flesh receives his wages in material blessings, like a hired worker with his master, who owes him his wages in return for his works, and the matter ends without any additional grace or justification; that is, he remains a sinner who is not permitted to enter the Kingdom of Heaven. And here, beloved, are examples of this.

The Hindus, who perform very great ascetic works according to the flesh, are rewarded by God with wages according to their works, but they did not receive justification or salvation, since they have no faith.
The Pharisee, who did all the good works, boasting of himself, went out from before God unjustified, and even more, fallen into the sin of self-righteousness and pride.

So works alone do not justify, because before God they are nothing, for He says, "When ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do" (Lk 17:10), although works are necessary after faith.

entries.section: (1) Abraham was justified by his faith

paragraphs.text: Worketh not: the works of the Law, or works in which he relies on himself that have no relation to his faith in God, like the works of unbelievers.
Believeth: in Christ the Redeemer of all sinners.
The ungodly: the one who persists in evil.
Is counted for righteousness: his sins are forgiven, and he receives the righteousness of Christ and entrance into the Kingdom.

The ungodly who has sunk into the depths of evil and whom every way failed to change, if he is broken before God, confessing his faults without seeking excuses for himself, and declaring his complete readiness to change his ways and obey his Master, and to begin the straight and earnest path with God, confident of His power able to remove his sins, this person is counted righteous before God.

entries.section: (1) Abraham was justified by his faith

paragraphs.text: Without works: he had no opportunity to work, but died soon after his faith. Or what is meant is the works of the Law, which the Gentiles did not do, but when they believed in Christ they received justification. As David says, blessed is the man to whom righteousness is imputed without works. The phrase "without works" does not mean that works are unimportant, for their great importance was already pointed out in (ch. 2:6), but what is meant here is the one who was not given the opportunity for works, like the good thief, who did all that was possible of faith and witness to Christ in his circumstances, as a bound man hanging helpless on the cross, but his life was not extended further to do good works. He reached Paradise, and so did many others of the martyrs of pagan origin, who, when they saw the miracles and crowns of the Christian martyrs, believed and were even martyred in the name of Christ, dying before time allowed them to do good works. These received justification by faith and the baptism of blood without works.

entries.section: (1) Abraham was justified by his faith

paragraphs.text: The Psalm (32:1) bears witness to the happiness of those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered through God's mercies.

entries.section: (1) Abraham was justified by his faith

paragraphs.text: Blessed is he to whom God does not impute his sins (Ps 32:2), for He forgets them as though they had never been, while the criminal in the world continues to be pursued by his crimes, always written in his record, counted against him even after he receives his full punishment.

How great is the grace of God, which forgives our sins in the sacrament of confession, opens to us the doors of prayer and speaking with Him at all times, gives us His word in our hands in the Holy Bible, and cares for us in all our steps. Let us lift up our hearts in constant thanksgiving to Him, and meditate at all times on His many gifts.

entries.section: (2) Abraham was justified before circumcision

paragraphs.text: St. Paul asks: does the preceding blessedness come upon the circumcision (the Jews) only, or upon the uncircumcision (the Gentiles) also? Of course it includes both.

entries.section: (2) Abraham was justified before circumcision

paragraphs.text: Then St. Paul brings the decisive proof of the unimportance of circumcision in justification, by reminding the Jews of a historical fact of clear evidence, namely that Abraham was justified by faith while in uncircumcision, about 14 years before he was circumcised in the flesh, and before the written Law, which came by the hand of Moses more than 430 years after God's promise to Abraham.

entries.section: (2) Abraham was justified before circumcision

paragraphs.text: Then after the justification, circumcision came as a sign of the justification and not a cause of it, so that Abraham might be the father of all those who walk in the same way of his faith and were not circumcised, that is, the Gentiles who believed in Christ.

entries.section: (2) Abraham was justified before circumcision

paragraphs.text: Also that he might be the father of circumcision (the Jews), not of those circumcised in the flesh, but of those who walk in the same way of the faith of Abraham when he was a Gentile, that is, before he was circumcised.

Perhaps what concerns us in the above is that we should not rely on an outward form, or on superficial, showy worship, or on charitable works we have done, nor boast that we are children of the martyrs and saints, but we must have inner purity and a believing heart that loves God, ready at all times for good works as an offering of the love of God, and so God rejoices in us and counts us His sons.

entries.section: (3) Faith is a condition for obtaining righteousness

paragraphs.text: St. Paul continues to prove his case by opening the door of salvation to all and not restricting it to the Jews by the Law, for the promise of salvation and the righteousness of faith was earlier than the Law and its works, because if salvation were restricted to the Law and its works, God's own promise would be nullified (God forbid) - "and in thy seed (that is, Christ) shall all the nations be blessed."

entries.section: (3) Faith is a condition for obtaining righteousness

paragraphs.text: The Law came bringing with it penalties for the one who does not carry it out, and every person who knows the Law became condemned for transgression, that is, violation of the rulings of the Law. So how do we escape that transgression so as to obtain righteousness?

entries.section: (3) Faith is a condition for obtaining righteousness

paragraphs.text: Thus God grants all mankind, who believe like the faith of Abraham, whether the Jews his children according to the flesh or the Gentiles, an equal opportunity to obtain the promise of righteousness, that is, God's pardon of our iniquities as a grace and a gift from Him, for we obtain righteousness not as a price in return for our faith, but as a great reward far beyond our deserts as human beings.

entries.section: (3) Faith is a condition for obtaining righteousness

paragraphs.text: Before God: in God's estimation.
Whom he believed: Abraham.
Scripture says plainly that God said to Abraham, "I have made thee a father of many nations," because God considers him a father of the Gentiles and the Jews.
Abraham's faith in God appeared in two situations:
1- (God, who quickeneth the dead) When he obeyed God by offering Isaac his son as a sacrifice, he stretched out the knife to slay him, fully convinced that God would bring Isaac back to life again.
2- (and calleth those things which be not as though they were) When he believed that he would have offspring (Isaac) even before he was born and existed.

Trust in the power of God, which is able to turn your weakness into strength, and if you fall into difficult sins He forgives you and turns you to holiness. Your faith will push you into positive action, not hindered by the multitude of your sins.

entries.section: (4) All things are possible to him that believeth

paragraphs.text: Abraham, against hope and natural logic and human thought, believed in hope in God's power and ability to raise up the Gentiles from the darkness of sin and the shadow of death to become His sons, when it was said to him by God: "So shall thy seed be," O Abraham, many as the sand of the sea and the stars of heaven.

entries.section: (4) All things are possible to him that believeth

paragraphs.text: Abraham was strong in his faith, and gave no consideration or importance to the scientific fact that says a man cannot beget children when he has become old, and the deadness (death) of Sarah's womb (Sarah's womb), that is, the cessation of the ordinary course of women with her and her inability to bear children for a long time. He did not doubt for one moment God's promise, but believed it and gave glory and thanks even before the promise was fulfilled.
Beloved, you who desire to be a friend of God, do not be troubled if His promises are delayed, and do not doubt, for they are certainly coming at the proper time.

And do not let material calculations and human logic hinder your faith, for you are dealing with a God who is able to do all things, and what is impossible with men is possible with Him alone. So trust in Him and do not fear.

entries.section: (4) All things are possible to him that believeth

paragraphs.text: Here God rejoiced in Abraham's trust in Him, and counted him righteous in that situation also.

These words were not written to tell a story about Abraham that has ended, but behold, God's call is open to all mankind in general, and to you in particular. Let there be in you faith in the great, Almighty God, for He who raised up Jesus Christ from the dead is able to raise you from the death of sin.

Christ was delivered to death to die in our place because of our sins, and rose from the dead to raise us with Him from material, earthly life to a life of righteousness and spiritual conduct, that we may become righteous.

If the devil wars against you and you fall many times, do not be troubled, but believe in the risen Christ, and offer repentance that He may forgive your sins, and continue your spiritual striving; indeed, let your prayers and readings increase to make up for what you missed, and advance a new step in the way of the love of God.
The righteousness of Christ saves us from sin and gives us good fruits

entries.section: (1) The fruits of the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: When we received justification by faith, which is the forgiveness of sins in Baptism and the beginning of a life of holiness by the Holy Spirit in the anointing of the Myron, we came to be at peace with God, and this reconciliation was accomplished through our Lord Jesus Christ. The faith here is the faith of the one baptized if he is an adult, or the faith of his parents if he is a child.

entries.section: (1) The fruits of the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: Through Christ also "we have access." The word "have" means that we were changed from the position of the sinner, rejected and driven away, to the justified, beloved one, called to enter the fold of Christ by faith, to enjoy the grace of redemption, then justification, then peace.
The phrase (we stand) means continuing to enjoy grace, and this is by means of the sacrament of repentance and confession, which is a renewal of Baptism.
And we also boast and rejoice in what we await of the glory that God prepares for us in heaven.

entries.section: (1) The fruits of the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: Tribulations, instead of being a source of the Christian's feeling of oppression and injustice, have become a source of pride and glory for him. Why? Because tribulations train us in patience and endurance.

entries.section: (1) The fruits of the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: The patient one is proved, that is, succeeds in the test of faith, since he did not doubt God during the trial, and the one who succeeds has hope that he will inherit eternal life, and everyone who has put his hope in Christ will not be disappointed. What makes us endure tribulations is that the Holy Spirit, poured out in our hearts, constantly assures us of God's love for us, so we fear no evil.

Do not look, beloved, at the bitterness of the tribulation, but at the tender hand of God that controls the tribulation, for nothing will befall you from it except what is for your good on earth and for your glory in heaven.

entries.section: (2) Christ the Righteous, Redeemer of sinners

paragraphs.text: We came to know God's love for us even more when Christ died for us, since because of our weakness we persisted in sin.

entries.section: (2) Christ the Righteous, Redeemer of sinners

paragraphs.text: Righteous: pure, with his sins forgiven. Good: pure and doing good works.

Human logic teaches us that scarcely will a person die for a righteous man occupied with worship and piety, or perhaps a person will die for a good man (who is more excellent than the righteous man in his service, his good works, and his giving of himself for others). But who is it that dies and sacrifices his life for an ungodly man, who does not deserve life at all?!!

entries.section: (2) Christ the Righteous, Redeemer of sinners

paragraphs.text: Here Christ shows the greatness of His love for mankind, when He, the Righteous, died for sinners like me and you.

entries.section: (2) Christ the Righteous, Redeemer of sinners

paragraphs.text: Just as Christ began our salvation with power when we were sinners, all the more will He complete our salvation on the heavenly level, so that we are spared punishment on the day of wrath (judgment), on condition that we walk in a life of righteousness and piety.

entries.section: (2) Christ the Righteous, Redeemer of sinners

paragraphs.text: Here St. Paul brings us to a logical idea, which is that since Christ, when He was dead in the flesh, was the cause of our reconciliation, we sinners, with the Father, then all the more, after we have received reconciliation, we receive salvation by growing in His love and cleaving to Him.
We shall be saved by His life: St. Paul reveals an important part of the work of salvation, which is the life of the Lord Christ Himself, and it includes:

His life in the flesh, which He lived on earth, in which He fulfilled all righteousness on our behalf, so that He became pleasing to the Father on behalf of our humanity, and became an example for us to follow.

His life in our body: when we partake of His most holy Body and Blood, He abides in us and we in Him. Then He works in us and through us good works pleasing to the Father, which become a cause of our salvation.

entries.section: (2) Christ the Righteous, Redeemer of sinners

paragraphs.text: Thus we rejoice and boast in our reconciliation with God, who ordered the moment of the salvation of mankind through His Son, whom He gave for us. And here St. Paul draws our attention to the fact that salvation is not the work of the Son only, but is also by the ordering of the Father, that we may rejoice and boast in the Father and the Son.

If you, my brother, have been reconciled with God, make use of His love by establishing a strong relationship with Him, being careful about your prayers, your meditations in His word, and going to His house (the Church), to strengthen your relationship with Him and even to experience new depths of His love. And let you have a renewed aspiration every day toward God.

entries.section: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: When Adam sinned by eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and despised God's clear warning, "in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die," he brought sin into the world for the first time, for it had been unknown before, and consequently he received the penalty of death. Adam bequeathed to his offspring the corrupt nature, which knows evil and is weak in resisting it, and death, as the wages of sin, passed upon all men. In another translation, the Jesuit translation from the Greek text, it says "in whom all have sinned" instead of "for that all have sinned," that is, all mankind were in the loins of Adam when he sinned, so they sinned in him, like a slave who married a bondwoman and they bore slaves.

entries.section: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: Is not imputed: its guilt is not shown and defined except by the Law, because man had warped the natural law within him, which is the conscience, by his distance from God. So he was no longer able to distinguish wrong from right.

Of course sin existed in the world from Adam until the coming of the Law, as proved by the existence of the wicked such as Cain and the people of Sodom... and so on. The wicked thought that God would not count their sins against them, because He had not yet sent down the Law (the statute) by which He would judge them. So they walked by the law of the jungle and deserved death, although they should have walked by the voice of God within them, which is the conscience.

entries.section: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: After the similitude of Adam's transgression: the same sin as Adam's, though their sins were less.

The righteous also died, who did not sin like Adam, the transgressor against God. And perhaps you, reader, ask: what then is the fault of the righteous like Noah and Abraham, who pleased God and whose sins were few and limited?

Here St. Paul reassures us that the justice and mercy of God will set things right with the coming of the One to come (Christ), who is like Adam in His effectiveness and influence upon all mankind. The first Adam bequeathed to us death through sin, and Christ bequeathed to us life through righteousness.

In verses (15-19) St. Paul will draw a comparison between the sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ, the sum of which is that the blessings Christ (the second Adam) brought us exceed by thousands of times the death through sin which Adam "the first man" brought us.

entries.section: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: If the sin of Adam has spread through the whole human race, the grace of Christ justifies those who believe in Him and fills their lives with holiness. That is, the grace of Christ is overflowing and sufficient for everyone who believes in Him.

entries.section: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: If Adam bequeathed his sin to mankind, the grace of Christ forgives not only the ancestral sin but all the sins that people have committed, and they receive a new, pure nature in Baptism, and indeed their sins are forgiven many times afterward in the sacrament of repentance and confession.

entries.section: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: Death reigned: all died because of the sin of Adam.
Shall reign by One: they receive the Kingdom through Christ.
The sin of Adam brought death upon all mankind, while the grace of Christ gives believers to reign forever with Christ in the heavens.

entries.section: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: Just as the sin of Adam spread in the human race, so the righteousness of Christ frees them from the final judgment and gives them eternal happiness.

entries.section: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: All inherited sin through the sin of Adam, while the obedience of Christ gives purity and new life to all believers.
Do not submit to sin, for it is an intruder upon us. Let us repent and enjoy the righteousness of Christ, and continue our striving in a spiritual walk until we reign forever in the heavens.

entries.section: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: By this it appears that Christ has the whole role in justification, and the Law has no role.
Why then did the Law come?

It came "that the offence might abound," that is, become clear, and to nullify the argument of mankind that sin is not imputed when there is no law (ch. 5:13). The Law came carrying a long list of prohibitions without any loopholes, to close to mankind the opportunity of falling into sins on the pretext that they did not know they were sins. So the Law was like a mirror that revealed to mankind the hideousness and multitude of its sins. But just as the names, forms, and kinds of sins multiplied through the Law, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ multiplied and surpassed and overflowed, so that it can forgive and blot out every iniquity however great.

If you live in difficult circumstances that try to keep you away from God, do not be troubled. Flee from them as much as you can, and be confident that the power of God supports you and keeps you with greater help than the one who lives in ordinary circumstances. That is, do not blame circumstances when you sin, but repent and ask God's help, and you will overcome sin however difficult or dominating it may be.

entries.section: (3) The sin of Adam and the righteousness of Christ

paragraphs.text: The conclusion is: if you, O man, are grieved because the sin of Adam brought us death of the body after the misery of life, although we are not directly responsible for Adam's eating from the tree, behold, Christ died for us without guilt so that we might inherit eternal life, if we walk in a life of righteousness by faith and works, relying on the grace of Christ.
Baptism and striving to obtain justification

entries.section: (1) The role of Baptism in justification

paragraphs.text: St. Paul condemns the opinion of the sinners who say that if God increases His grace and mercy toward those who have fallen into severe sins and difficult circumstances in order to help them come out of them, then let us remain in a life of sin to receive God's many mercies.

entries.section: (1) The role of Baptism in justification

paragraphs.text: Dead to sin: by Baptism.

St. Paul denies this opinion, because if God in His abundant mercy poured out upon us His rich graces to remove from us every trace of sin, this does not push us to carelessness and persisting in sin. Then he explains that by Baptism we have become like a dead being in relation to sin, so that when it attacks us it finds in us no senses to be seduced and no members to carry out sin.

entries.section: (1) The role of Baptism in justification

paragraphs.text: Were baptized into Jesus Christ: received Christian Baptism, in faith in Christ the Savior. Were baptized into His death: the more exact translation is "was baptized in His death," that is, he dies with Christ when he goes down into the water of Baptism and rises with Him.
The value of Baptism is very great, because in it we die with Christ to our sins. By His death He took away our sins and saved us from them.

entries.section: (1) The role of Baptism in justification

paragraphs.text: By Baptism we share with Christ in His death and His resurrection, which was accomplished by the glory of the Father (by the power of the Father), so we are buried that the old man, weak before sin, may die in us, and then we rise as a man born anew, walking in newness of life with a holy conduct. So life by Baptism is like the process of creation.

entries.section: (1) The role of Baptism in justification

paragraphs.text: The likeness of His death: immersion in the water of Baptism, which resembles the death of Christ on the Cross.

We shall be also in the likeness of His resurrection: we live the life of resurrection and victory over sin and enjoy fellowship with Christ. When we were baptized and sin died in us in a form like the death of Christ on the Cross, we were united with Him in a close union, so our self became one with His, and we enjoyed the joy of the resurrection with Him. That is the first resurrection in our life, when sin dies in us and we live to righteousness, as the Lord Christ said about the prodigal son: "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found" (Lk 15:24).

entries.section: (1) The role of Baptism in justification

paragraphs.text: The old man: the old corrupt nature inherited from Adam, inclined to evil. The old man died with Christ in a mysterious way when He was crucified on the Cross. And by the death of the old man, "the body of sin" was destroyed, that is, sin became no longer in force over us, because we died in relation to it.

This reminds us of the saying of St. Augustine, when a woman came to him after his repentance, who had been accustomed to practice sin with him in a past time, and he said to her, "The Augustine whom you knew is dead." By this man is freed from the dominion of sin over him, and does not become its slave.

entries.section: (1) The role of Baptism in justification

paragraphs.text: Also he is freed, that is, there is no longer anything that binds him to sin, and it no longer has dominion over him, and its relationship with him has ended.

entries.section: (1) The role of Baptism in justification

paragraphs.text: Just as we shared with Christ in death when we were buried in the water of Baptism, so we rise with Him with a new holy nature that does not incline to evil, as He rose with a body of light.

entries.section: (1) The role of Baptism in justification

paragraphs.text: What makes us confident of our spiritual resurrection in Baptism is that we believed there is a resurrection, because Christ has risen from the dead and will never die again, since He is a holy, living God who does not die, but died by His own will for our sins, and then rose to live in oneness with the Father. Thus everyone who is baptized dies to sin and lives in righteousness to please God.
The phrase once points to the fact that Baptism is not repeated, just as Christ also died once.

Remember at the beginning of every day your new nature which you received in Baptism, that you may live a new life for Christ, seeing Him before you in every work and word to please Him and to offer love to everyone you meet.

entries.section: (2) The human role in justification

paragraphs.text: After St. Paul drew our attention to the divine factor in the process of salvation and justification, he moves to the human factor, advising you, after you have become clean, wearing the garments of salvation, not to return again to being soiled in the mud of sin, but let your members become living members to carry out God's will in you.

You who have been freed from the slavery of sin, do not return to sell yourself cheaply to it and become its slave again, obeying its commands over your body, which has gone back to desiring the pleasure of sin. And why, after Christ put to death in you, in Baptism, the various passions, do you return to bring them to life again, stirring and activating them with your senses when you expose them to external influences and stimuli, so that you descend once more to the bottom of sin?

entries.section: (2) The human role in justification

paragraphs.text: Baptism frees you from the dominion of sin but does not give you immunity from error. If your body is dead to sin, why do you stir it with passions until sin reigns over it a second time?

entries.section: (2) The human role in justification

paragraphs.text: Do not make your members doers of sin. Do not make your tongue abusive, nor your hand striking, nor your body fornicating as though it were an animal body stripped of reason and wisdom; rather, offer yourself, which is your soul, your thought, your mind, and your heart, as a living person aware of the value of your soul and as a son of God who does righteousness with all the members he has been given (praying / serving)...

entries.section: (2) The human role in justification

paragraphs.text: In this way sin will not be able to lord it over you, because you are not in the age of the Law, which was limited to rebuking man for his sins without giving him any power to overcome, but you are now in the age of grace, the grace of the Holy Spirit who works in you with a mysterious power, and the love of Christ that surrounds you, and the care of the Father who helps you. And in this your members are strengthened, and you overcome and triumph.

entries.section: (3) The servant of sin and the servant of Christ

paragraphs.text: Strangely, some in the age of grace misused their understanding of the freedom that is in Christ, and turned to license. Here St. Paul strongly condemns the baptized, purified person walking in evil.

entries.section: (3) The servant of sin and the servant of Christ

paragraphs.text: Man, as the Lord Christ said, "No man can serve two masters" (Mt 6:24), is either an obedient slave to sin in its commands over his body, and the result will be spiritual death for him and man becomes like an animal body; or he is obedient to God's commandments, and so becomes righteous.

Beware, beloved... for your obedience to sin is obedience to the devil himself, who gives deceptive names to sin to lessen its impact on a person's conscience lest he repent, such as calling fornication the sins of youth, anger strength of personality, and greed ambition... and so on.

entries.section: (3) The servant of sin and the servant of Christ

paragraphs.text: Which you received from the apostles: here St. Paul points to the importance of the apostolic tradition as a source of teaching alongside the Gospel.
You obeyed from the heart: this makes clear that Christianity is not outward moral commandments but love from the heart, which leads to obeying His commandments and walking in the commandment.
The form of doctrine: this affirms that the teaching depended on an example seen in the lives of the teachers, and not merely words or theoretical preaching.
Here St. Paul thanks God, not because they lived as slaves of sin, but because they left that way and followed with all their hearts the teachings of Christ which they received from the apostles.

entries.section: (3) The servant of sin and the servant of Christ

paragraphs.text: When you were freed from sin, you became servants, by your own free will, of God, carrying out His commandments.

entries.section: (3) The servant of sin and the servant of Christ

paragraphs.text: I speak after the manner of men: that is, in an easy, simple human style, so that souls weak toward sin may understand it.
Unto iniquity: out of love for it.

Since you readily accepted slavery to sin, and your members were doing uncleanness and iniquity out of love for it, the time has now come for the members to become holy, working righteousness, so that you become saints.

entries.section: (3) The servant of sin and the servant of Christ

paragraphs.text: There are two main ways:
a- The way of evil and passions; whoever walks in it becomes a slave of the devil, free from the commandments of Christ.
b- The spiritual way; whoever walks in it is a servant of his Master Jesus Christ, the King of Peace, freed from any dominion of sin over him.

Satan comes, beloved, deceiving and saying: Come, be free from all the restraints of the commandment. Why do you weary your body with fasting? Why do you deprive your body of pleasure, enjoyment, and sin? Why do you guard your tongue from error?

So come, do what is pleasing in your eyes, free from the commandments of the Gospel that lead to righteousness. But you, beloved, as soon as you obtain this false, so-called freedom, find yourself leaving the righteousness of the compassionate God who loves mankind, who gives peace on earth and eternity in heaven, and entering under the dominion of cruel Satan who hates mankind, so he humiliates and shatters your life and your future and even your eternity.

entries.section: (3) The servant of sin and the servant of Christ

paragraphs.text: Then St. Paul returns, posing a question: what fruit did you have as a result of this former life, in which you did evils of which you are now ashamed? And because you repented of them, you were delivered from eternal death, that is, the punishment of Gehenna.

entries.section: (3) The servant of sin and the servant of Christ

paragraphs.text: But now, after you have been freed from sin and have become beloved servants of God, you have received the fruits of the Holy Spirit, "love, joy, peace... and so on," and then God will reward you in the end with eternal life.

entries.section: (3) The servant of sin and the servant of Christ

paragraphs.text: Then St. Paul comes to the sum of life: if you commit sins and do not repent of them, you will die an eternal death. But to the one who walks in righteousness God gives eternal life, which our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ opened before us.
Christ frees me from the Law and saves me from sin

entries.section: (1) Through Christ we were freed from the Law

paragraphs.text: In this chapter, since it was difficult for the Jews, who had lived many years keeping the traditions of the Law, to give it up suddenly after the resurrection of Christ, St. Paul began to prove that the Law with its ordinances no longer has dominion over man. He addressed his words to the Jews who knew the Law, expressing astonishment that they had forgotten and been ignorant of the fact that the Law is laid down only for the living, meaning that a person is obliged to carry out the rites of the law of Moses only as long as he is alive, since death nullifies any contract between two parties.

entries.section: (1) Through Christ we were freed from the Law

paragraphs.text: St. Paul gave an example of this, which is the woman's obligation to the law (the statute) that binds her to her husband as long as he lives; she cannot leave him and marry another man unless her husband dies, and then she is free from the law that regulates her marital relationship with that man.

entries.section: (1) Through Christ we were freed from the Law

paragraphs.text: The woman, during her husband's life, cannot be joined to another man or she would be called an adulteress, but if he dies she can be joined to another man and in this case is not called an adulteress.

entries.section: (1) Through Christ we were freed from the Law

paragraphs.text: So you also, Christians of Jewish origin: the Law regulated the relationship between you and the old man, that is, your nature inclined to evil, just as the law binds the woman, who signifies your souls, and the man, who signifies the old man.

The Law and the commandments are like the bridle that restrains your instincts and abilities, so that they do not swerve after the old man, who is inclined to evil. And when the old man died with Christ on the Cross, the soul was freed from the dominion of the old man over it and from the Law, and became free to be joined to another, who is the new Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ, with His new statutes and laws for it in the New Testament. The fruit of this marital union is the fruits of the Holy Spirit and good works.

entries.section: (1) Through Christ we were freed from the Law

paragraphs.text: The flesh: that is, that in which the old man works, namely the nature inclined to evil. By the law: by which the Law shows its ugliness and evil.
In the Old Testament, when people lived in the flesh inclined to evil, the evil passions, whose ugliness the Law shows, worked in man. And so his fate was death and going down to Hades.

entries.section: (1) Through Christ we were freed from the Law

paragraphs.text: Wherein we were held: united with it in our body.

Now, after the completion of redemption and the death of the old man, that is, the nature inclined to evil that worked in the man in whom we were held, we were freed from him and from the Law that governed our relationship with him, and we were joined to Christ, and we have a new relationship with Him regulated by a new rule, which is the worship of God in the Spirit, and not the formal relationship of the literal application of the Law.

Do you gladden God's heart by rising from formal worship of the flesh to the release of the spirit and its soaring in heavenly things in a relationship of mutual love with God? Then your fasting becomes not only of the body, but you rise above material things and outward shows that magnify living, so that your prostration with the body is in humility and contrition in spirit, and your prayer is deep and burning with love for your heavenly Bridegroom.

entries.section: (2) The Law reveals sin but does not save from it

paragraphs.text: The matter became confused for some people, who thought that the Law and sin are one thing, on the grounds that we were freed from both at the same time after Christ. Certainly the Law is not sin; God forbid that this be true. The Law made known to me sins of all kinds and forms, but it forbade me from them. The Law said to me, "Thou shalt not covet," and instead of keeping away from desire and rejoicing in God's commandment, I desired sin more, acting on the psychological principle that says (the forbidden is desired).

entries.section: (2) The Law reveals sin but does not save from it

paragraphs.text: The commandment revealed sin, and the soul clung to it instead of leaving it; that is, the commandment revealed evil to me, so I sought it and clung to it. And the phrase "without the law sin was dead" does not mean that sin did not exist, but the meaning is that before the Law man committed sin as something natural in his daily conduct, not knowing that this conduct was sin; that is, he thought sin did not exist, as though it were dead, and then the Law came and revealed his sins.
Man's failure to recognize sin before the Law was because man had warped the conscience by which he distinguished wrong from right, so he needed the Law to guide him and reveal sin to him.

entries.section: (2) The Law reveals sin but does not save from it

paragraphs.text: St. Paul confirmed his words by saying that before the Law man practiced sin as an ordinary thing, killing, cursing, stealing, and getting angry, and he lived in the flesh, that is, he lived a fleshly, animal, unspiritual life and was content with his state. The law of Moses had not yet come to reveal his sins and count them against him, but when the commandment came with the Law, man realized his predicament and said to himself, "I am surely lost and I shall die because of my sins."

And the phrase "sin revived" does not mean that it was dead and then lived, but the meaning is that man was able to recognize it through the Law, so it was revealed and became alive, and at the same time man's fault and his deserving of death appeared.

entries.section: (2) The Law reveals sin but does not save from it

paragraphs.text: The commandment, which was supposed to rescue man from a life of sin to a life of holiness, stood only as a dry statute, since the Law did not stretch out its hand to help man to be delivered from sin, being content only with holding him accountable and then sentencing him to death.

entries.section: (2) The Law reveals sin but does not save from it

paragraphs.text: The commandment made me know sin, so Satan intervened to make sin attractive to me, and sin deceived me, as I thought it would satisfy my needs and make my life easy, so I fell into it and was sentenced to death; that is, sin slew me.

entries.section: (2) The Law reveals sin but does not save from it

paragraphs.text: The Law is holy, just, and good because it is words that came out of the mouth of the holy God, and the wise man loves the Law, understands it, and applies it, but the fool who twists the commandments to suit his desire deceives himself and falls into sin and death.

entries.section: (2) The Law reveals sin but does not save from it

paragraphs.text: The Law cannot be blamed as the cause of the fool's conduct in evil and then his death, just as a judge cannot be blamed and described as a murderer if he sentences a criminal to death. Consequently, the goodness of the Law cannot become a cause of death except for one who wanted for himself disobedience to the Law and twisting its commandments. How cunning is Satan!
