We note that every believer must stay with his gift and not go beyond its field into the field of another gift. For this reason St. Paul repeats his saying, with the gift in the same kind of gift, such as "he that ministereth, on ministering."

entries.section: (2) The kinds of gifts in the Church

paragraphs.text: Fourth, exhortation: this is advising others and guiding them how to walk in the path of virtue and to behave as befits children of God. Thus the teacher addresses the mind while the exhorter addresses the heart and the will, so that both may move the body and soul toward holy spiritual conduct.

Giving: this speaks of the virtues that he wants all believers to enjoy, unlike the gifts that are given to only some. The virtues are necessary for a person's salvation, while the gifts are for the service of the Church. Giving in the world's understanding is tied to expecting something in return, such as a wage or reward, but giving in the Church is with liberality, that is, in abundance and without expecting anything in return, to the point that a person offers his whole self to others.
Then he returns, a second time, to the gifts and speaks about:

Fifth, ruling with diligence: ruling is the organizing, arranging and distributing of responsibilities in the ministry, and guiding, directing and supporting everyone. And why diligence? Because Church matters must be taken with seriousness, depth and wise thought, not hasty or superficial. The ruler is diligent, that is, he is not content with the role of adviser, but works in the field of service with his own hands and shares with others in their work and labors.

Then he continues his long discourse on the virtues and speaks to us about mercy, which in the world's understanding is only exempting the wrongdoer from punishment, whereas spiritual mercy is cheerfulness, that is, showing love, warmth and heartfelt forgiveness to the wrongdoer, and accepting him as a living, active member serving in the Church.

If we are members of one body, then may you value the service of every person, however small it may seem, and encourage him with kind words. At the same time, do not despise any small work that you offer, confident that God cares about it. And if you are doing a great service, do not become proud, because it is a grace given to you for the sake of others, lest God withdraw it from you, however gifted you are, in order to save you from your pride.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: Love: how many relationships in this world are classed under the title of love, such as emotional love in words only without any self-giving, and love that expects something in return for a personal interest or benefit. All of these are certainly unacceptable before God, and therefore they are called hypocritical love.

But true love without hypocrisy is that which springs from the heart in limitless self-giving, and this has an abundant reward from God. The one who has this love finds himself hating every evil. For we cannot do evil except to one whom we hate, and when we love a person, we find that we do all possible good for him with wonderful spontaneity. Therefore love has become inseparable from doing good.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: Kindly affection: this is different from the world's "courtesy," in which people flatter one another in various ways that are all formal. True kindly affection springs from a loving heart, showing itself in offering and honoring the other. The word "kindly affectioned" means that we take the initiative in showing affection to others, so that we are not only receivers of affection.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: We must be diligent: to acquire the virtues, and when God sees our striving, He rewards us with spiritual fervor and zeal in our relationship with Him, so that we worship Him sincerely. The reverse is also true: when we worship the Lord and pray to Him much, the fervor of the Spirit is kindled in us, and this leads us to diligence in spiritual matters and practical virtues without laziness.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: Patience and hope during tribulation: on our journey toward eternity many tribulations confront us, whose aim is to hinder us, wound us and make us fall. Therefore St. Paul offers the solution, which is rejoicing in hope, that is, looking to the glory that is about to be revealed in us. For tribulation is our field for gain and for winning the heavenly reward, if we succeed and persevere in prayer, as though we were saying that nothing separates us from the love of Christ, and so we find great help and strength from God supporting us.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: Giving to the needy and the stranger: and how beautiful is the title that St. Paul gave to the poor, for they are the saints because of the hardship of life they endure, and the injustice of the rich and the harshness of the proud toward them. He also means by the saints the believers who are sanctified in Christ. The word "distributing" means that every member of the body must share in this service to his needy brother. Therefore the early Church lived a life called the "life of fellowship," in which there were no natural differences, for all were satisfied.

"Given to hospitality": the word "given" means constant care for these strangers. And strangers are not only those who need to be cared for materially, but also psychologically, for many suffer from isolation and a feeling of loneliness, either because people are too busy for them or because of their moving from one country to another, and they need someone who shows them care and love.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: Blessing those who wrong us: here St. Paul raises us step by step to the summit of the mountain of the commandments, which is dealing with those who wrong us. His commandment "curse not" may be acceptable, but how can I bless and pray for good for one who persecutes me, wrongs me and takes away my rights?! The answer is that sin is weakness, so the one who persecutes me has fallen under the hand of the devil, and I must pray for him that God may rescue him, and praying for him changes his heart so that he becomes a member like us in the Church, as happened with St. Paul himself. And I bless the persecutor, because his persecutions will become medals on my chest before Christ. In wars of old, the brave soldier felt proud of his wounds and his amputated limbs, which he bore with honor.

In sum, we have compassion on those who wrong us because sin is weakness, we accept tribulation from the hand of God because it is for our good, and we overflow with the divine love dwelling in us, so we bless them and pray for them.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: Then St. Paul directs us to share in the other's joy, that is, to rejoice for him from my heart without jealousy and without envy, and my sharing in the expressions of his joy must be within limits that do not grieve the Spirit of Christ dwelling in me. Although the person in the world today refuses to share in the other's sorrow because he simply cannot bear the other or even listen to his sorrows and cares, the spiritual person is always a tender bosom, a listening ear and a gentle, comforting tongue.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: Humility: our sharing with one another in joy and sorrow makes us one body with one concern, which is eternal life, not concerned with the material things of the world and the grandeur of living ("high things"), but it leads us to be drawn to the lowly, that is, to imitate the humble saints and follow their example. Among the virtues of the humble person is that he listens, learns, obeys and submits, whereas the proud "wise man" is the one who walks according to his personal desires and opinions, not submitting to guides or priests or the Church or even God Himself. True wisdom is in submission to God and to guides, whereas the one who is wise in his own eyes is the proud, so his wisdom is false and mere cleverness or information, but he cannot act well, because wisdom is good conduct.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ abolished the idea of repaying the other in kind, that is, evil for evil, because the believer's nature has become love for everyone, even those who wrong him. Not only that, but the Christian must not be a cause of stumbling by any wrong conduct of his before people, but must always act with propriety, courtesy and gentleness, so that the world may see the good image of the children of God and glorify Him.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: "Live peaceably": this means that I, as a Christian, strive to make peace, which is reconciliation with all people with a pure heart, on my own initiative, and I do not wait for the other to come to me. The peacemaker is a positive person, not weak or passive.
And why did St. Paul say "as much as lieth in you"?

Because there are people who may refuse to make peace with me without any cause from me, merely because I am a Christian or because of some evil in their hearts, and here I am innocent of this quarrel, which is on their side only, while my heart is open to loving them even if they insist on boycotting me.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: Without doubt the wronged soul fights with anger and the desire for revenge, and here St. Paul, like a wise physician, directs the believer to a psychologically and spiritually healthy way of dealing with this anger and this desire for revenge, saying, "give place unto wrath," that is, let God be angry in your place, and in His anger He will avenge you, for God is just and He alone has the right to repay because He is without sin. So we leave God, the wise Father, to discipline and teach His children what is good, while I pray for those who wronged me, and in this our resentment toward the wrongdoer ends, and there will be no room for gloating over him if the hand of God stretches out to discipline him; on the contrary, he is then in a position that calls for pity for him because of God's vengeance.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: Therefore if you know that your enemy is hungry and in need, give to him and help him, or if he is thirsty, give him drink. In this you will force him to be ashamed of himself, and he will review his conscience, rebuke himself and repent, as though by your love you had put a fire burning in his head, burning up his wrong thoughts toward you, so that he returns and loves you.

entries.section: (3) Virtues in the Christian community

paragraphs.text: That is the means of overcoming evil, not by answering it with evil but by doing good. We overcome the proud with our humility, the angry with our gentle words, and the thief with our embracing him.

You, beloved, are called to acquire all these virtues so that you may truly become a son of God, and their sum is that you love every person, feel his need and strive to help him. And in proportion to your practical love you receive inner peace and a blessing from God in all your steps.
The duties of the Christian in society, and his repentance

entries.section: (1) The duties of the Christian toward society

paragraphs.text: Christianity lived, in most of its ages, under the rule of non-Christians, and here St. Paul points out that authority is good in general, because it is a social order for regulating life and relations among people, and this is better than primitive societies dominated by chaos and the rule of gangs. God rejoices in authority because He is a God of order and not a God of confusion, for authority is an arrangement that God approves for ordering society, and the Apostle commands us to submit to it and respond to it.

entries.section: (1) The duties of the Christian toward society

paragraphs.text: Whoever resists authority, that is, rejects it, opposes it and fights it, is as though he resists God Himself, and also exposes himself to earthly judgment, that is, the punishment of the rulers. Even in the ages when rulers resisted and persecuted the Christians, what was required was submission, which reached the point of martyrdom, which was by God's permission since it was a cause of blessing and of the spread of Christianity. Therefore Christianity, throughout its ages, did not allow revolutions or riots against the states or authorities that persecuted it, but endured the persecutions with bravery, courage and joy.

entries.section: (1) The duties of the Christian toward society

paragraphs.text: We return once more to ordinary systems of government, that is, those that do not persecute Christianity, where the Saint says that government and rulers are not a terror or a punishment to those who do good, but a cause of fear and discipline for evildoers, such as thieves, murderers, bribe-takers, forgers, and so on. Therefore whoever wants to live in peace under any system of government should do good, that is, what is required of him or permitted by the laws of the state, and so become a good citizen.

entries.section: (1) The duties of the Christian toward society

paragraphs.text: "The sword": punishing the wicked by death.

The one in authority is a minister of God, whom He established to judge justly among people, so that security, justice and tranquility prevail in society, and thus society is purified. For this reason St. Paul gives advice to everyone who does evil, so that:
First, he may not enter the circle of fear, anxiety and punishment from the rulers.

Second, because our Christian conscience, which loves humility, obedience and self-giving, is satisfied with nothing but carrying out the commandment of Christ to submit to the authorities. Christianity is a peaceful religion, not an objecting, resisting or troublemaking one. This does not mean that a person should not demand his right or defend it, but let him demand his right by sound, logical ways and not by crooked methods or illogical argument. For in the ages of persecution great defenders appeared who defended the Christian religion with all their strength.
If we are required to submit to our unbelieving rulers in the world, how much more should we submit to our spiritual shepherds, such as priests and guides, and to our fathers and mothers.

entries.section: (1) The duties of the Christian toward society

paragraphs.text: If the Christian submits to the authorities in everything that does not conflict with God's commandments, it is obvious that this means submission in simple matters such as paying tribute, that is, taxes, because they pay for public services for the whole society. And although the Church has blessed giving to the needy ("the necessity of saints"), she counts the tax collectors as God's ministers who collect contributions to serve others, as well as the public services that all citizens enjoy.

entries.section: (1) The duties of the Christian toward society

paragraphs.text: "Tribute": a tax on persons or property, given to the collectors of tribute.
"Custom": a tax on trade goods, given to the collectors of custom.

The Lord Christ Himself gave us an example when He paid the tribute and said, "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's" (Lk 20:25). Everyone must receive his due, and we must show respect to everyone in a position, with esteem and fear and not out of hypocrisy or opportunism, so that we fear evil and do not do it out of fear of its punishment, and likewise we honor those in positions in the state with the customary honor for these ranks, so we confirm our agreement with and submission to the order of society, which is useful for keeping everything in check.
You, beloved, should review your stance toward your superiors, and ask yourself.
1- Am I faithful in what is required of me, or am I lazy and negligent in my work?
2- Do I demand my right by upright ways if I am wronged, or do I perhaps resort to crooked or violent ways to take my right?

entries.section: (2) Loving every person in the world

paragraphs.text: The Apostle Paul commands the Christian to love others in society, because God has put overflowing love in the heart of every Christian to distribute it to others as though it were a debt on him that he is bound to pay to others, because the Christian is the light of the world, a refuge for everyone weary and a tender bosom for everyone in need of love. The Christian must not owe anything to anyone, that is, take something material or moral from people and not return it, because in this he would be like a thief.
The Law is divided into two parts:
a) A part concerning commandments toward God.

b) A part concerning commandments toward people (Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, and so on), and the sum of it is that you love your neighbor as yourself. Note that the Lord Christ interpreted the meaning of the neighbor, in the parable of the Good Samaritan, as any person in need in the world.

entries.section: (2) Loving every person in the world

paragraphs.text: Whoever loves someone cannot do him harm, and the one who has love finds that he does not sin against any of the commandments of the Law, that is, he is perfect in all the commandments of the Law, for love is the fulfilling of the Law.

Therefore, beloved, if you have fallen into many sins, or are failing in your spiritual exercises to resist sin, know that the easiest and shortest way to obtain the virtues is love. Purify your heart from resentment and hatred, and then the virtues will flow into your heart one by one until perfection.

entries.section: (3) Repentance now, before time is lost

paragraphs.text: The Apostle Paul warns us not to waste time in the pleasures of the world or in vain things, for we do not know how much of our life remains. Every day that passes brings us closer to meeting Christ, and death may come to us sooner than we imagine, or Christ Himself may come in His Second Coming at any time. So let us rise and leave the works of darkness, which are evils, and do the works of light, which are the virtues. He likened virtue to armor because of its power for victory over the enemy's attacks.
He likens our life on earth to the night for the darkness, gloom and weariness in it, and our meeting with Christ in Paradise to the joyful, happy day.

Note, beloved, the beauty of the verse "The night is far spent," for it gives comfort to everyone weary that every evil and injustice will soon pass away. So endure with thanksgiving from the hand of God, confident of the eternal reward, and you will also receive peace and comfort on earth.

entries.section: (3) Repentance now, before time is lost

paragraphs.text: "Rioting": merrymaking with insolence.
"Chambering and wantonness": all kinds of adultery and perversion.

Let us walk in fitting works and good conduct as though we were in the day, that is, as though everyone sees us. It is not right for us to indulge in evil desires. It is strange that he added strife and envying after grave sins like adultery, to make clear that all of them deprive us of the Kingdom.
One of the gentle exercises for leaving sin is to ask myself:
Would I have done this sin if people were seeing me now? And the more important question: can I do this sin while God sees me now?
So train yourself to be aware of God's presence, as Elijah the prophet says, "As the Lord liveth, before whom I stand" (1 Kgs 17:1), and by this you will keep away from every sin.

entries.section: (3) Repentance now, before time is lost

paragraphs.text: "Provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof": the inclination and planning to carry out evil desires and the body's indulgence in worldly pleasures.

But the greatest means of overcoming sin is to "put on the Lord Jesus Christ," that is, always meditating on the life of the Lord Jesus, following the conduct of Christ, being united with Him and abiding in Him in the sacrament of the Eucharist, and being satisfied with His love, tenderness and care, and in this we will not find in ourselves an inclination to the lusts of the flesh, and we will not be able to anger God. Caring for the weak in faith and not causing them to stumble

entries.section: (1) Receiving the one who is weak in faith

paragraphs.text: After St. Paul laid down the foundations of faith among Christians of Jewish origin and of Gentile origin, here he solves a secondary problem in order to put an end to every division in the Church. He found that there were two groups: one he called the weak in faith, who are mostly Christians of Jewish origin, influenced by their former worship in that they did not eat certain foods such as pork, considering them unclean for them. He called them weak in faith because they were still bound by the letter of the Law with a measure of scrupulosity. He commanded that no one from the second group, who eat everything with thanksgiving, should despise them, and also that the weak in faith should not judge the strong in faith for eating everything, for God has received both groups as they are.

entries.section: (1) Receiving the one who is weak in faith

paragraphs.text: Then he addresses both groups, that neither should judge the other, because they are both servants of God, and God alone is responsible for each one, since He receives each one and establishes each one in Him, for He is able to do so.

Pay attention, beloved, to your discussions, for how much of your time and the time of others have you wasted in foolish debates, arguments and inquiries whose aim is to prove yourself and that please Christ in no way, but make you fall into much judging.

entries.section: (1) Receiving the one who is weak in faith

paragraphs.text: Some Christians of Jewish origin held fast to the feasts of the Jews at the beginning of Christianity, and these have spiritual meanings, such as the Day of Atonement, that is, the redemption of Christ, and the Feast of Tabernacles, which means the world's being a place of exile, and so on. The other group, that is, the Christians of Gentile origin and the rest of those of Jewish origin, lived these meanings every day, because the Christian feasts had not yet been fixed at the beginning of the apostolic age, except the feast of the Resurrection. Likewise the first group did not eat certain foods forbidden among the Jews, while the other group ate everything with thanksgiving for God's sake. So the Apostle Paul asks all of them that neither should judge the other, for the purpose of all is good, which is drawing near to God.

entries.section: (1) Receiving the one who is weak in faith

paragraphs.text: What matters is that a person lives to please God by good works and not himself, that is, his personal opinions, and even if he dies, he dies in the faith, pleasing God. He made clear that God accepts differences between individuals, if the purpose is to please God, but calmly. In this he protects the Church from individualistic tendencies that could lead to the division of the Church, if they are tied to pride and to not submitting to her teachings and guidance.

entries.section: (1) Receiving the one who is weak in faith

paragraphs.text: Life, in all its details, for the believer is nothing but an offering of the love of God, in which he tries, as much as he can, with the capabilities and energies he has been given, to please God and be faithful in his talents. The Christian is strong; he does not fear death but welcomes it, since it is his goal, because it will lead to seeing Christ in heaven.

entries.section: (1) Receiving the one who is weak in faith

paragraphs.text: The plan and design of the Lord Christ, when He died, rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, was to reign by love over the hearts of the believers on earth and of those who have triumphed in heaven.

entries.section: (1) Receiving the one who is weak in faith

paragraphs.text: St. Paul returns, saying to the group weak in faith, "Do not judge your brother," and saying to the group strong in faith, "Do not despise the actions of the one weak in faith," but let each one turn to himself, rebuking himself for his own sins, because every person of every race or religion will bow and stand before the throne of Christ, giving an account of himself and his own works, not the works of his brother.

Judging distracts you from your repentance, so examine yourself every day and begin spiritual striving, and through the labors of striving you will feel the weakness of others and their need for your prayer instead of judging.

entries.section: (2) Do not cause the weak in faith to stumble

paragraphs.text: Instead of despising the weak, let our chief concern be not to cause him to stumble by our eating things unclean in his sight, knowing that there is no unclean food in God's sight, but it is unclean only from the viewpoint of the one who counts it unclean, that is, in the sight of the one weak in faith.

entries.section: (2) Do not cause the weak in faith to stumble

paragraphs.text: "Grieved": stumbled. If the law of love for the other is the highest of the Church's laws, then we must not insist on eating or doing things that grieve your weak brother, who is precious in God's sight because Christ died for him. So for God's sake do not eat in front of him and do not cause him to stumble, lest he doubt you and think you sinful, saying that you are not righteous and that you violate the commandments of God, though in truth you are righteous and live in the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

If you are connected with the Church or serve in it, you must care for those who are far away, and not do in front of them things that they could misunderstand and so be caused to stumble because of you, because you are a model and example for them, and they do not expect error from you and seek to be like you as an angel. Likewise parents should be mindful of their conduct in front of their children; their anger and quarreling, for example, is very distressing to the children.

entries.section: (2) Do not cause the weak in faith to stumble

paragraphs.text: Because the Kingdom of God, which is within us and which we live with Christ, is essentially love, joy and peace, it is not right for us to be occupied with discussions or stumblings concerning eating and drinking. Has not the Church arranged long fasts throughout the year to protect us from preoccupation with food and to give us more heavenly things?

entries.section: (2) Do not cause the weak in faith to stumble

paragraphs.text: "These things": love, joy and peace. Let our first aim then be to please Christ by making love and peace, and in this also people will commend us, that is, praise us, so that we become a good example that gladdens them and not a stumbling block from which they recoil.

entries.section: (2) Do not cause the weak in faith to stumble

paragraphs.text: So it is good that we not squander our energies on what does not benefit the Church, but work and watch with all diligence to establish peace among the members of the Church and prevent divisions. Let all our speech be not for tearing down the other and proving our point of view right, but let us speak spiritual words that build him up spiritually and make him grow in Christ, for "he that winneth souls is wise" (Prov 11:30).

entries.section: (2) Do not cause the weak in faith to stumble

paragraphs.text: The work of God, which is the salvation of souls and their spiritual edification, is far more important than food. It is not right to destroy the work of God so that you may eat in your freedom and cause your brother to stumble, because this conduct would be evil on your part and you would become evil in the sight of God.

entries.section: (2) Do not cause the weak in faith to stumble

paragraphs.text: It is better for you not to eat meat nor drink wine, nor anything that could cause your brother to stumble.

entries.section: (2) Do not cause the weak in faith to stumble

paragraphs.text: You will say to me, "But I believe that this food is not unclean." Well, then eat it, but not in front of people weak in faith, only by yourself before God, and then your conscience will be at rest and will not condemn you in the eating that you consider good and not unclean.

entries.section: (2) Do not cause the weak in faith to stumble

paragraphs.text: But the one who eats something while doubting and not confident in the rightness of what he does, it is better that he not eat it, lest sin be counted against him.
Our love for others, and Paul's longing and praise for the Romans

entries.section: (1) The strong in faith is the one who bears with the other

paragraphs.text: St. Paul begins his chapter with a verse that sums up the previous chapter, which is that the one who is strong in his faith and in his love for God gives up what comforts and pleases himself so as not to burden the one weak in faith, and even bears with long-suffering and takes in with a wide heart the thoughts and opinions of those weak in faith. This is contrary to the thinking of the world, which supposes that the one who bears with others is a weak person without personality.

This is fulfilled in practice when the servant, or parents, humble themselves before the one served or the children, listening to their opinions calmly and with love without attacking them or silencing them with big words, and in time they will find the opportunity to correct some wrong concepts calmly.

entries.section: (1) The strong in faith is the one who bears with the other

paragraphs.text: So let each one think how he will win the other without selfishness. But to what extent should I please the other? The deciding factor is the good and righteousness, meaning that servants accept the opinions of the one served or the opinions of the other as long as they do not conflict with what is good and right, and it is never required that the Church concede, be lax and become careless about concepts that may lead the one served to destruction, or else the Church would lose her holiness, become like the world, and lose the one served forever as well.

entries.section: (1) The strong in faith is the one who bears with the other

paragraphs.text: Although the world today teaches a person to live pleasing himself with extreme selfishness even if the other is harmed, the Lord Christ did not teach us this, but looked to what pleases us, that is, salvation and redemption, and bore sufferings and insults for our sake, so that He cried out to the Father, saying, all the insults that those who reject You want to say to You have insulted Me with while I am crucified on the Cross.

entries.section: (1) The strong in faith is the one who bears with the other

paragraphs.text: The previous verse and all the verses of the Old Testament were written not as history, but so that we may learn how to walk spiritually by suffering for the sake of others. For the word of God written in the Holy Bible comforts us and gives us patience in our sufferings, so that we can bear the sufferings of the present in the hope that our labors will turn to glory in the end.

entries.section: (1) The strong in faith is the one who bears with the other

paragraphs.text: God promises to support His children with patience and inner comfort, so that they continue in their love for all and in seeking their salvation.

For the one who pleases another at his own expense, God opens to him unlimited energies and countless compensations, and even patience itself becomes easy. How many times have we heard in the rich history of our Church of saints who bore with others with patience and joy.

entries.section: (1) The strong in faith is the one who bears with the other

paragraphs.text: "One mind": feelings of love that bring all together.
"One mouth": one thought and one teaching.
In this you are rid of division in the Church, and you become one mind and one mouth, and thus the name of Christ is glorified when the world sees His children as one unity without division.

entries.section: (1) The strong in faith is the one who bears with the other

paragraphs.text: If the holy, perfect Christ received us, defiled sinners, despite the vast difference between us and Him, how much more should we, weak sinful human beings, receive our weak brothers with love, whatever their condition or mistakes.

Do not forget your one goal, which is the salvation of yourself and others. Give up your comfort and desires to win those around you. For in the midst of our selfish world, the love that everyone needs shines forth. Offer your love, even with a smile or a small word of encouragement, and pray for all.

entries.section: (2) Receiving the Jews and the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: "The circumcision": that is, the Jews.

The Jews and the Gentiles are equal in that Christ served both by offering them salvation, not because of any merit in them. He saved the Jews because of His promise to their fathers that He would save their descendants despite their many disobediences, and as for the Gentiles, the prophecies (Ps 18:49) and (Deut 32:43), which St. Paul cites in (vv. 9, 10) respectively, had already indicated that God would have mercy on them because He is a God of love, mercy and compassion, even though they were unworthy because of their many sins.

entries.section: (2) Receiving the Jews and the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: "A root of Jesse": the Lord Christ. "To reign over": your King.

He also affirms the joy of the Gentiles because God saved them, as it came in (Ps 117:1). Not only that, but the Lord Christ will be your King (Isa 11:10), that is, He will reign over your hearts and thoughts, and the state of enmity between you and Him will end and turn into hope in Him, that is, confidence that He loves you and saves you. He specified the Gentiles in the two verses (vv. 11, 12), to erase from their hearts any sense of inferiority in comparison with the Jews.

Among the greatness of God's mercy is that every person is placed in God's plan of salvation, even those far away who were not given the opportunity of spiritual teaching in their youth. A day will come when the grace and work of God visits them with power, and has mercy on them and brings them back to His embrace if they wish. So take care to show Christ to those far away, invite them to the Church and pray for them however evident their evil, for God seeks their salvation and is able to turn them into saints.

entries.section: (2) Receiving the Jews and the Gentiles

paragraphs.text: Finally St. Paul prays for them that the grace of the Holy Spirit may support them, so that they may stand firm and their hope and certainty in Christ increase, and they rejoice in their life with God and feel peace.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the Romans

paragraphs.text: In humility, the Apostle Paul praises the Romans so that they would not think that he is being harsh with them and counts them sinners, but he makes clear that in his eyes they have reached a high level of goodness and knowledge, and that among them are people of a high degree of holiness, who are able to counsel and rebuke the wrongdoers among the Romans for their salvation.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the Romans

paragraphs.text: "The more boldly": Paul dared and spoke of new depths in the faith, since he saw that the level of faith of the believers in Rome could bear this deep speech.
"In some sort": in some parts of the epistle.
Why then did the Apostle write to them?
To remind them of some truths of the faith, and this is a gentle and humble approach from Paul, to regard his words as a mere reminder to them because they know everything.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the Romans

paragraphs.text: This perfection makes them without blemish. Then he said that only here can I, Paul, the minister to the Gentiles, stand before Jesus Christ like the priest who offers sacrifices. But instead of offering a holy offering of fine flour and without blemish, I offer you to God, since your heart, your mind and your life have been sanctified by the Holy Spirit and have become worthy to be offered to God like the offering without blemish.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the Romans

paragraphs.text: When I say that I am the minister to the Gentiles, do not think that I am boasting of myself, for all the glory and boasting goes back to Christ Jesus, who strengthened me for the ministry to the Gentiles, which became my portion by the plan of the Father.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the Romans

paragraphs.text: I do not dare to attribute the credit to myself, because all the credit goes back to the work of Christ in my words and deeds, so that the Gentiles might return to obeying God.

entries.section: (3) Praise of the Romans

paragraphs.text: "Illyricum": northwest of Macedonia, in present-day Greece.

Christ performed miracles and wonders through me, the weak one, by the power of His Holy Spirit, so that God was able to work through my weakness and bring the Gospel to the region lying between Jerusalem and Illyricum.

Note, beloved, that the more the servant humbles himself and feels his weakness, the more God works through him many powers and wonders. So thank God after every work you do, and ask His help before everything.

entries.section: (4) The limits of ministry

paragraphs.text: "Christ was named": Christ had been preached.
"Another man's foundation": one of the apostles who had preached in a place and founded a church there.

I was careful to preach in regions where the Gospel had not reached before by another apostle, so as not to rob the other apostles of their rights. For each apostle has a region in which to preach and reap its fruit. This is precision and humility on Paul's part in respecting the feelings of the other apostles, but it is not wrong for two apostles to preach in one place.

Although cooperation among servants is beneficial and necessary, on the other hand let each servant have his own ministry on which he concentrates, lest he trouble the other with his interference. So look for the neglected ministry or the souls far away, and do not run after ministries that are visible and praised by others out of love of appearing.

entries.section: (4) The limits of ministry

paragraphs.text: The Apostle Paul acknowledges that he preached in places that had not heard of Christ before, and by this they saw and heard of Christ, in fulfillment of the prophecy of Isaiah (Isa 52:15).

entries.section: (5) Paul's longing to visit them

paragraphs.text: Paul wished many times to visit Rome, but each time he was hindered from visiting them, but now, since he has finished preaching in and visiting the regions he intended in his plan, nothing remains but Rome to visit. Therefore he will come to them, and after he is filled with them in part, he will set out to Spain, since he will never be filled with them.

entries.section: (5) Paul's longing to visit them

paragraphs.text: Before Paul comes to Rome, he will first go to Jerusalem to minister to the needy believers, since contributions have been collected from the regions of Macedonia and Achaia, which are Gentile cities, to be given to the people of Jerusalem, and this is love and generosity on their part. But from his viewpoint this is considered a return of favor, for just as the Jews shared their spiritual things with the Gentiles, so the Gentiles share with them in material needs.

entries.section: (5) Paul's longing to visit them

paragraphs.text: When he has finished this offering, which is the fruit of the Gentiles' love for the Jews, he will pass by them on his way to Spain.

entries.section: (5) Paul's longing to visit them

paragraphs.text: When he comes to them he will find them at a high degree of spiritual life filled with blessing, since they will have left their divisions and trained in acts of love and in receiving the other.

entries.section: (5) Paul's longing to visit them

paragraphs.text: In humility and need he asks them to pray for him and with him diligently and persistently, because he is about to face a hard trial, which is confronting the unbelieving Jews in Jerusalem, who will devise plots against him, and this is what actually happened afterward. And he asks for prayer not in order to escape hardships, for hardships do not matter to him, but he prays that the ministry, which is the desire of his heart, may succeed, and that the people of Jerusalem may accept the offering of love presented by the Gentiles.
Therefore the Church always prays for her shepherds, the Patriarch, the bishops, the priests and the servants, that the Lord may complete their ministry.

entries.section: (5) Paul's longing to visit them

paragraphs.text: In this my heart rejoices at the completion of the ministry and at meeting you, which I longed for.

entries.section: (5) Paul's longing to visit them

paragraphs.text: Finally he prays for them that God may be with them in all matters of their life, He who is the King of peace, the Giver of peace to all who follow Him.

Take care to offer love to everyone in need, so that you become accustomed to doing good, and even long to meet every person to give him your love. Then the love of God and His mercy will overflow upon you, and your giving will increase until your whole life becomes love for everyone.
Greetings from Paul and his companions to the believers in Rome, and a warning against false teachers

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: "Phebe": a name meaning radiant. She was a deaconess in the church of Cenchrea, which is the port of the city of Corinth (in present-day Greece). It appears that Phebe was wealthy and loved to give, and she spent her money to serve many, including Paul himself, so he asks them to appreciate her and help her to complete her service. And he places Phebe at the head of the list of those to whom he sends greetings, before the men, because she was distinguished above all in her love and service. There is no distinction between man and woman before God except in love.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: "Who have for my life laid down their own necks": Paul faced severe persecutions that threatened his life, and this couple defended him and exposed themselves to death for Paul's sake. Perhaps this was in hosting him or accompanying him.
"All the churches of the Gentiles": they helped Paul in his ministry to the Gentiles in many lands, so they deserved to be thanked by them.

Note here the mention of the wife Priscilla before her husband Aquila, because she was more zealous for the ministry. They were Jews who were expelled with the Jews from Rome, so they went to Corinth and received Paul in their house, and helped him in his ministry to the Gentiles, so the churches of the Gentiles such as Rome ought to honor them.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: Because of the persecution of the Christians in the apostolic age, they were compelled to hold the Liturgies and prayers in houses, being unable to build church buildings. It appears that the house of Aquila and Priscilla was a center where the Liturgies were held, so Paul sent his greeting to the company of believers who attend this church that is held in their house.
Paul continues his discourse and greets Epaenetus, who was the first to believe in the region of Achaia, in present-day Greece.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: "Mary": a Jewish woman who rendered many services to the Church, and the Apostle Paul, by his greeting to her, shows his appreciation of her deeds.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: "Andronicus and Junia": two Jews who believed in Christ before Paul, and labored in the ministry until they were imprisoned, and bore many tribulations. They are related to Paul by kinship.

"My fellowprisoners": they were imprisoned with Paul during his preaching, and the time or place of this imprisonment is not mentioned because Paul was imprisoned many times (2 Cor 6:5). "Of note among the apostles": known for their love and distinguished service.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: "Amplias": one of the well-known believers in Rome. With overflowing feelings Paul describes him as his beloved.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: "Urbane": one of the well-known servants, and he describes him as a helper in Christ, that is, one who does not seek his own glory but the spreading of the name of Christ.
"Stachys": one of the believers beloved to Paul.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: "Apelles": a Christian famous for virtue.
"Aristobulus": a well-known wealthy person, but a pagan, and therefore Paul did not greet him. "Them which are of Aristobulus' household": probably his slaves or relatives who had become Christians.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: "Herodion": a Jew, so he calls him my kinsman, and there may be a close or distant kinship between them. "Narcissus": he was a slave who believed and was freed, then was martyred for the name of Christ, and his household, that is, his relatives, continued their strong spiritual life with God, so the Apostle Paul sends them greetings and encouragement and praises them because their life is connected with God.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: "Tryphena and Tryphosa": two maidservants who believed in Christ and served Him. As for Persis, she is an old woman who served the Lord. He calls her the beloved because of her giving and her abundant love.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: "Rufus": the son of Simon the Cyrenian, and his mother showed care for the Apostle Paul, so he calls her his mother.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: Paul mentions a group of names of Christians, some of whom were slaves and were freed, and there was with them a company of Christians. It appears that groups of Christians had formed in various parts of Rome, each group worshiping God in a strong Christian life.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: Philologus and Julia, husband and wife, and their children Nereus and his sister Olympas: this family was part of another Christian company in Rome, to whom Paul sent greetings and love.

entries.section: (1) Paul's greetings to the believers in Rome

paragraphs.text: He sends them greetings and love in the form of the apostolic kiss, as the deacon calls out in the Liturgy, saying, "Greet one another." This means forgiveness and love so that we may be prepared for Christ to dwell in us. And the churches of the Gentiles send greetings to the Church in Rome, which is the capital of the empire.

How beautiful is the bond between the members of one Church, and between the different churches. Offer your love to all your fellow believers, for love creates a path of cooperation and encourages holding fast to Christ amid the tribulations of life.

entries.section: (2) Warnings against false teachers

paragraphs.text: "Divisions": that is, thoughts outside the one true faith that they learned from the apostolic teachings.
"Offences": that is, one does right things but causes others to fall into sins, since they understand the action in a wrong way and doubt and so are kept away from God.

St. Paul asks the believers to watch, as guards, with caution anyone who tries to create divisions or offences in the Church, so that they may preserve the level of love and the one unity in the Church.

entries.section: (2) Warnings against false teachers

paragraphs.text: "Their own belly": their personal gains and private aims.
"The simple": the peaceable and kind.

Why should we mark them? Because they are not obvious. They slip into houses and into the midst of the Church, claiming to be her children, and they speak general Christian words, sweet and good, with outward holiness and deceptive kindness, so many are deceived by them and follow them, and it is not long before they inject their poisons like vipers, and kill many spiritually among the peaceable and kind who love everyone and suspect no one. Their aim in this is material gain, since houses open their doors to them with food, drink, hospitality, money and fame, and they certainly have no connection with the service of Jesus Christ.

entries.section: (2) Warnings against false teachers

paragraphs.text: You are famous for the obedience that I love in you, but let this virtue be only for the one who deserves obedience, that is, the Church, and not for the innovators who think you are easy prey for them. Therefore even the good, that is, obedience, should be with wisdom and discernment, but as for evil, be simple in it, that is, as though you were children who do not know it and do not deal with it or experience it.
Beloved, do not open your ear or your house to anyone who claims to be from the Church, but verify his identity with great care.

entries.section: (2) Warnings against false teachers

paragraphs.text: So by our unity, our fighting against heresies and our love, we will overcome Satan and he will be crushed, because our Lord Jesus Christ fights for us, and Satan falls defeated under our feet, those that strive and labor, not the lazy feet. And in this Christ overcomes Satan through us.

Look, beloved, at the power of God, who holds your right hand to fight the devil, so do not fear his wars and evil temptations, because the One who is with you is your victorious God, who has already crushed Satan in the battle of the Cross.

entries.section: (3) Greetings from Paul's companions

paragraphs.text: Out of St. Paul's love and humility, he did not want to be the only one with love for them, so he pointed to others who have the same love for the Church of Rome, as though he were saying that without them he could not have completed my epistle. These who are mentioned are the servants accompanying Paul. Among them is Timotheus, the closest of Paul's disciples to his heart, to whom he wrote two epistles. And Lucius is a person other than Luke the Evangelist, while Jason was Paul's host when he preached in Thessalonica, and Sosipater is probably the one mentioned in (Acts 20:4), and these are relatives of Paul.

entries.section: (3) Greetings from Paul's companions

paragraphs.text: "Tertius": the writer of the epistle. Paul did not write by himself because of the illness of his eyes. Tertius also sends his greeting to the believers in the Church of Rome.

entries.section: (3) Greetings from Paul's companions

paragraphs.text: "Gaius": the host of St. Paul while he wrote the epistle, and he opened his house to the believers. "Erastus": who worked as the one in charge of the state's storehouses in Corinth.
"Quartus": perhaps he had no great position in society, but he was as a brother to St. Paul, for he values every person however simple.

Therefore, beloved, the servant must not be the only star beloved to those he serves, but he should point to the others who labored with him or served with him. So encourage and praise everyone who shares with you in the ministry, appreciating every labor, even if it is small.

entries.section: (3) Greetings from Paul's companions

paragraphs.text: Paul prays for the people of the Church of Rome that the grace of Christ may accompany them and dwell in them, so that they may be able to fulfill the commandments of his epistle, and understand and stand firm in its teachings.

entries.section: (4) The conclusion of the epistle

paragraphs.text: "The mystery": the acceptance of the Gentiles into the faith.
"Eternal times": in the thought of God before the foundation of the world.

God is able to establish the Gospel thought that I taught you, which is that Christ Jesus accepts the Gentiles into His Church together with their brothers the Jews. This thought was a mystery, that is, not accepted or understood among the Jews at that time, but God has now revealed it to us in the New Testament, so that I may preach to the Gentiles that they may have a share in the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

entries.section: (4) The conclusion of the epistle

paragraphs.text: The prophets of the Old Testament had already prophesied of the entering of the Gentiles, but the Jews did not understand that in the past. Now it has become known, evident and understood by all. The entering of the Gentiles into faith is not according to Paul's personal thought, but because it has been God's command from eternity that the Gentiles would obey the faith.

entries.section: (4) The conclusion of the epistle

paragraphs.text: Here is the sum of the epistle: that our wise and loving God allowed the entering of the Gentiles by means of the atoning work of Christ. To Him be the glory, for He arranged for us the plan of salvation. Amen.
"By Phebe": either she took part in writing a portion of the epistle with Tertius (v. 22), or she delivered this epistle by her own hand.

The love of God seeks the salvation of all, so do not despise anyone or be annoyed with him, for he may be a vessel that God will fill at the right time, even if this seems a mystery hidden from people for many years. So pray, and encourage everyone to be bound to God.
